articles.title: We're releasing the weights of Mistral Large 4
articles.content: We release the weights of Le Chonk, advancing the frontier of open models in agentic coding and cybersecurity. Earlier this month, we released Mistral Large 4 (Le Chonk), our flagship 1-trillion-parameter, natively multimodal model, in public preview. The response to the preview has exceeded our expectations, and we're grateful to our developer community, early-access customers, and partners for their support, collaboration, and feedback. Since then, we've put that feedback to work while continuing to scale reinforcement learning, driving massive improvements in coding and defensive cybersecurity . Gains continue to accelerate, with no signs of saturation. Today, we're releasing the weights of this improved Mistral Large 4. The new model also features substantial gains in reasoning efficiency that give developers greater performance while lowering inference costs. Mistral Large 4 ranks as the best open-weight model for coding and among the world's most capable open models overall. Trained from scratch on European infrastructure with clear lineage from inception to release, it gives organizations a trusted foundation for Sovereign AI Mistral is defining the sovereign AI category and leading the open frontier. We're committed to building the world's most capable models and releasing them openly, giving developers, enterprises, and institutions the power to own, customize, and control their AI. Built for the Builders. Mistral Large 4 entered public preview with strong results across leading coding benchmarks. Just three weeks of additional reinforcement learning have since propelled it to the forefront of open-weight coding, taking the lead on FrontierCode and Terminal-Bench while matching the best open-weight models on the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index with substantially greater token efficiency. On Cognition's private FrontierCode 2.0 benchmark, which assesses end-to-end code quality and whether a repository maintainer would merge the agent's change, Mistral Large 4 leads with a score of 19.7%. Cognition - FrontierCode 2.0 0.0% 5.0% 10.0% 15.0% 20.0% 19.7% 2.9% 14.2% 17.3% 17.8% 19.3% Mistral Large 4 Beam 1.0 GLM-5.3 Flash Kimi K3 GLM-5.3 DeepSeek V4.1 Flash Score Pushing the pareto frontier for agentic coding. Mistral Large 4 delivers frontier coding performance with significantly fewer tokens, making sophisticated coding agents more economical to run at scale. On the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index, Mistral Large 4 scores 48%, effectively tied with the leading open-weight model, GLM-5.3, while using 47% fewer tokens per task on average. articles.title: A tiny world model running games on a Raspberry Pi Pico 2 W
articles.content: Using 2 small neural networks to generate and play the game at the same time on a Raspberry Pi Pico 2 W. The first one creates the game: given the current frame and the action, it predicts the next frame and the reward. The second one plays that game: it uses the generated frame and picks an action. Every frame above was sampled by the world model network, and the actions were taken by the actor network. I got interested in looped transformers, where one transformer block is applied several times with the same weights instead of stacking different layers. Reusing weights is cheap on memory, so I wanted to see if a looped world model could be small enough to run on a microcontroller. I picked the Pico 2 W because it is cheap and has an FPU, and small games because I could write the real versions directly into numpy and check every generated frame against them. Later I added a streaming RL agent so the board could also learn to play inside its own dream. Contents: the two networks · the games · the world model · the agents · quantization · on the chip · flashing · browser · reproduce · code layout The world model and the actor network 1: the world model network 2: the actor job frame + action → next frame + reward frame → action architecture looped transformer, q int8 MLP with two hidden layers, float32 size 26k–131k parameters 9k–16k parameters cost per frame 2–8M multiply-adds 9k–16k multiply-adds trained on recorded real games ( how ) with stream-x, in the real game or inside the dream ( how ) The size depends on the game, some games require more parameters to learn them to be playable, we tried to get to keep the number of the parameters small enough. On the chip neither network ever uses the real game: the actor only sees frames the world model, and the world model only gets actions from the actor. Both run on core 1 of the RP2350, while core 0 handles USB and the display. The pretrained actor can be swapped for a fresh stream-x agent that learns from scratch on the board. And any button press hands control to you, so you can play the dream yourself. Each game is a few hundred lines of numpy in src/tinyworldformer/games/ . It renders to a small grid of token ids, and one frame always holds the whole game state, so hidden state has to be drawn into the frame: the ball's heading is part of its token, and Doom-lite has a minimap. game frame rules random event world model exact frames, 2 loops Breakout 20×16 paddle, ball, 56 bricks, 5 lives the serve after a miss 26k params, 4.3M MACs 99.99% Doom-lite 32×32 raycast first-person view of an 8×8 maze; an enemy walks shortest paths to you; you shoot the enemy's respawn 55k params, 4.2M MACs 83.6% (see below) Flappy Bird 24×24 gravity, flaps, scrolling pipes the next gap height 46k params, 2.0M MACs 100% Pong 20×32 you against a CPU paddle that reacts late, first to 5 the serve after a point 46k params, 2.3M MACs 99.45% Pac-Man lite 48×48 23×21 maze, 249 pellets, two ghosts on shortest paths, 3 lives t

articles.title: H.264 Is Magic (2016)
articles.content: H.264 is a video compression codec standard. It is ubiquitous - internet video, Blu-ray, phones, security cameras, drones, everything. Everything uses H.264 now. H.264 is a remarkable piece of technology. It is the result of 30+ years of work with one single goal: To reduce the bandwidth required for transmission of full-motion video. Technically, it is very interesting. This post will give insight into some of the details at a high level - I hope to not bore you too much with the intricacies. Also note that many of the concepts explained here apply to video compression in general, and not just H.264. Why even compress anything? A simple uncompressed video file will contain an array of 2D buffers containing pixel data for each frame. So it's a 3D (2 spatial dimensions and 1 temporal) array of bytes. Each pixel takes 3 bytes to store - one byte each for the three primary colors (red, green and blue). 1080p @ 60 Hz = 1920x1080x60x3 => ~ 370 MB/sec of raw data. This is next to impossible to deal with. A 50GB Blu-ray disk will only hold ~2 mins. You can't move it anywhere fast. Even SSDs have trouble dumping this straight from RAM to Disk[^1]. So yeah. We need compression. Why H.264 compression? Yes, I will answer this. But first let me show you something. Here is the Apple Homepage: I captured the screen of this home page and produced two files: Eh. What? Those file sizes look switched. No, they're right. The H.264 video, 300 frames long is 175KB. A single frame of that video in PNG is 1015KB. It looks like we're storing 300 times the amount of data in the video. But the file size is a fifth. So H.264 would seem to be 1500x as efficient as PNG. How is this even possible? All right, what's the trick? There are very many tricks! H.264 uses all the tricks you can think of (and tons you can't think of). Let's go through the important ones. Shedding weight Imagine you're building a car for street racing. You need to go faster. What is the first thing you do? You shed some weight. Your car weighs 3000 lbs. You throw away stuff you don't need. Those back seats? pfft. Chuck those. That subwoofer? Gone. No music for you. Air Conditioning? Yeah, ditch it. Transmission? Ye..no. Wait! We're gonna need that. You remove everything except the things that matter. This concept of throwing away bits you don't need to save space is called lossy compression. H.264 is a lossy codec - it throws away less important bits and only keeps the important bits. PNG is a lossless codec. It means that nothing is thrown away. Bit for bit, the original source image can be recovered from a PNG encoded image. Important bits? How does the algorithm know what bits in my frame are important? There are few obvious ways to trim out images. Maybe the top right quadrant is useless all the time. So maybe we can zero out those pixels and discard that quadrant. We would use only 3/4th of the space we need. ~2200 lbs now. Or maybe we can crop out a thick border around the edges of the frame, the

articles.title: LLM Voice
articles.content: Sometimes when I read a post, I get the growing feeling that I'm reading the output of an LLM. I can't necessarily define why, although there are the common tells (it's not the em-dashes, it's the load-bearing tapestries). As I do this my desire to read on atrophies, sometimes to the point of revulsion There are tools out there that claim to be able to tell the difference between LLM-written prose and the old-fashioned biological product. I'm wary of them, partly due skeptism about their accuracy, but also because it rather misses the point. The reaction to LLM-Voice is a human one, that sense that we are in an uncanny valley of prose. By the time I'd reach for a tool to tell me what I'm reading, it's already too late, even if it confidently tells me there's no LLM present. I'm also suspicious of my own ability to accurately recognize LLM voice. Language changes over time, so a common sign of age is complaining about the language of the youngs. I'm inclined to bristle at prose that talks about “adopting a new sales motion ,” or “a sharp round-up of news”. But I've heard these constructs coming out of human mouths, so that's more a generational difference rather than between carbon and silicon. (And as a transplanted Brit, don't get me started on Americanisms, I'm sure I'll get used to them momentarily.) Right now I urge authors to be extra-wary of LLM-Voice. In particular I strongly recommend that authors should not fall into the trap of getting the LLM to write a draft. Even if it's edited by a human, it's very hard to expel the LLM-Voice - thus causing the uncanny valley reaction. Even accepting suggestions of rephrasing is dangerous. I have heard of people using LLMs to develop outline and structure, that may be ok, but only as far as an outline. Authors should fill the prose themselves. Say Your Writing is even more important in the age of LLMs. I habitually speak the words in my head and then write them down (and then edit what I've just written). This advice is particularly important to anyone who has any desire to communicate regularly with writing. Like many things, learning to be a good writer relies on lots of practice. It's a skill worth the time to acquire, but surrendering to an LLM will undermine any progress. In time it may be that LLMs will be so good that we can't tell the difference. In many ways, that's more worrying. Like most writers, I find writing an almost-essential tool for thinking. Often it's only by writing something down, that I can really get my thoughts on a topic into coherence. I've often started an essay knowing I don't really understand something, but the act of wrestling with the words forces me to overcome my confusions. As more people delegate writing to LLMs they will also delegate thinking and comprehension to LLMs. I don't want to do that, where's the fun of writing then? Although avoiding LLM-Voice is a general rule, it isn't an absolute one. An important example is that of Jim Highsmith (who contributes

articles.title: DoorDash to acquire Instacart
articles.content: Transaction values Instacart at $65.00 per share, representing a 26% premium to Instacart's closing price on October 22, 2026 Together, DoorDash and Instacart would help stores of every size reach more customers with the kinds of innovative technology that the biggest online retailers and grocers build for themselves Consumers to benefit from more choice and access to affordable delivery and savings Dashers and Shoppers to have more earnings opportunities and more choice over when and how they earn DoorDash, Inc. (NASDAQ: DASH) and Maplebear Inc. (d.b.a. Instacart, NASDAQ: CART) today announced a definitive agreement under which DoorDash will acquire Instacart for a total value of $65.00 for each Instacart share, or an equity value of approximately $17 billion. The aggregate transaction consideration will be at least 75% cash, with Instacart stockholders able to elect cash, DoorDash stock, or a combination of both, subject to proration so that DoorDash stock does not exceed 25% of the aggregate consideration. Instacart's board of directors has unanimously approved the agreement. DoorDash and Instacart share a mission to help local businesses succeed. Families turn to Instacart for the big weekly shop and to DoorDash for meals and nearly anything else they need from their neighborhood in under an hour. The combined company will offer grocers and retailers of every size DoorDash's delivery network and Instacart's grocery and fulfillment technology, in both apps and on stores' own websites, along with the advertising and AI tools each company has built. On either app, customers pick a store in their own community, and the store makes the sale. Consumers will have more stores to choose from, more savings opportunities when they choose to shop with a local business, and faster delivery options, while Dashers and Shoppers will have more ways to earn. Most grocery shopping still happens in stores, but more people are buying groceries and everyday goods online. They expect fast, affordable delivery and an easy way to order. The biggest online retailers and grocers are racing ahead, building their own delivery fleets, warehouses, membership programs, and AI shopping assistants. A grocer or retailer running on thin margins cannot build all of that alone, and with AI, the playing field risks being tilted even further away from local commerce. DoorDash and Instacart believe that communities benefit when Main Street competes, and they build the tools that empower local businesses. Together, they could help local stores grow online. More grocers could deploy Instacart's technology to run their own websites and retail media networks, bringing them more sales and advertising revenue. Brands would gain a scaled alternative for reaching customers online. articles.title: Chained PHP2Shell exploit roots 25 servers, including US Government servers
articles.content: Updated: October 29, 2026. Since this discovery, the Dream research team has been sharing updates and collaborating on an investigation with Palo Alto Networks, the vendor of the firewall in question. More information is available on the Palo Alto Networks website . Additional details are now included in the post itself. Custom PHP2Shell Exploit Chained with Kernel LPE to Root Versions of Palo Alto Networks PAN-OS Firewalls in the Wild On October 25, Dream researchers uncovered artifacts of what appeared to be a Chinese AI-assisted campaign that rooted 25 servers, including systems in a US government-affiliated environment. The attacker combined PHP2Shell with a kernel privilege-escalation exploit to compromise exposed systems. The affected devices run specific versions of Palo Alto Networks PAN-OS. The exploited surface is the PAN-OS management web server, which also fronts the GlobalProtect portal. Palo Alto Networks’ Unit 42 has independently verified the attacker’s tooling and results, and Palo Alto Networks is releasing fixed PAN-OS versions across the affected branches. After rooting the firewalls, the attacker launched attacks against Active Directory. The recovered artifacts confirm credential extraction and directory enumeration. The operation illustrates how an exposed management interface can become a path into an organization’s identity infrastructure. For government defenders, vulnerability discovery is just the beginning, after which the real challenge extends from identifying vulnerable systems to understanding and containing the access a compromise makes possible. The research below was conducted with proactive threat hunting using Dream’s autonomous cyber research product, Hero . Discovery Dream researchers identified a complete attack operation that included a custom weaponization of the PHP2Shell exploit chain (CVE-2026-109618/CVE-2026-109619) paired with the Fragnesia kernel privilege escalation (CVE-2026-46300), target lists, exploitation logs, and approximately 40 custom post-exploitation scripts. This included artifacts of a campaign that had rooted 25 PAN-OS firewall and management servers across the United States, Japan, Taiwan, and South Korea. Once rooted, the attacker zeroed in on three specific servers in a US government-affiliated environment. The discovered artifacts revealed an operation that began with exploit development in a lab environment and ended with persistent access to a US government organization's internal Active Directory domain. AI Usage in Attack We also observed some evidence of AI-assisted tooling in the attack infrastructure: Claude Code had been installed An AI-powered offensive security platform called aiscan was configured with Chinese LLMs DeepSeek and Kimi API keys for the Chinese reconnaissance platform FOFA were present While we have no direct evidence that the AI tools were specifically used to write the exploit or the post-exploitation scripts, the code structure, commenting style, and co

articles.title: What the fox say?
articles.content: I don’t remember playing this game when I was young, but it was a favourite of my wife’s late grandfather, and that half of her family knows it well. It is common wisdom in her family that the fox player needs to blunder badly for the sheep to win. Her entire family believes the game is heavily tilted in favour of the fox. I have played the game a few times, and indeed it has been easier for me to win when playing as fox. I have an unhealthy relationship with strategy games like these. I simply must put them through computer analysis to figure them out. I don’t know why. It’s just something that happens. I used to write tree search algorithms manually, but I have realised that OpenSpiel provides a generic tree search supporting most of the things I’ve ever found myself needing to support, so I can write the game rules in Python and hook into OpenSpiel to analyse it. Well, consider the rules above. How often do you think the fox wins, between two equal players? Write down your guess, and you’ll learn how good your sense of this is. I didn’t realise it right away, but what happened in that high search budget game was that we learned something about the nature of Starve the Fox . The sheep side requires deeper thinking than the fox side to play well. Since the sheep, in isolated conflicts with foxes, are so underpowered, they must move the mass of the entire flock in coordination to beat the foxes , and with one movement per turn, that requires strategising over many turns. 3 In fact, the sheep player isn’t really moving sheep as much as they’re moving the holes in the flock to make sure the holes stay away from the sheep closest to the foxen. This is a fantastic property of the game, because it (a) is thematically smashing, and (b) means a child can play an adult and both still have fun; the child gets to play the fox side and the adult just has to think harder. However, I didn’t want to wait for 16,000 iterations or whatever’s needed for the plain mcts to play a very strong game. One of the more expensive parts of that search algorithm are the random rollouts to score leaves in the search tree. A trick to make leaf scoring faster is to cut off the rollouts well before the game ends 4 The depth at which to truncate rollouts depends on both the complexity of the game and the quality of the rollout policy. For completely random rollouts, it may even be desirable to cut them off at depth zero – i.e. not perform any random moves at all, because they make the scored state less representative of the end state than the earlier leaf node was. In the case of Starve the Fox , stopping the rollout after 8 plies seemed to yield the best results with the first draft of the heuristic function, but it’s possible with a stronger heuristic function shorter rollouts would be even better, because they buy time for more tree search at the cost of not evaluating as far into the future. , and then use a heuristic function to score the positions in games that haven’t yet

articles.title: My favourite PowerMac is a Nintendo Wii
articles.content: (This is a guest post by Rairii) Mac OS 7.6 booting on the Wii Mac OS 9.2.2 booted on the Wii So today I reached a nice milestone in one of my projects: my work porting classic Mac OS to PowerPC systems with what I affectionately call ArtX chipsets (Nintendo GameCube, Wii, eventually Wii U; the GameCube’s Flipper integrated chipset was very much designed by ArtX as it was effectively finished when ATI acquired the company, and the Wii’s Vegas (and its later revision Bollywood) and Wii U’s Latte are effectively straight successors) reached the desktop for the first time, most likely the first time since the CHRP clone era that someone outside of Apple brought up classic Mac OS on a new system to the desktop. Despite still being nowhere near ready for a public release, I want to talk about the challenges I faced with this project so far. But first, why port classic Mac OS to this hardware in the first place? I’d already ported NT of course, and during that work I acquired some PowerPC Mac laptops which I also ended up porting NT to, work on one port improved the others and so on. This got me acquainted with the classic Mac OS, and I fell in love with the jank as it were (hacks upon hacks upon hacks going back to the 1980s is something I’d definitely describe as “jank”). Not to mention the m68k part of the TBXI is called “SuperMario”, and was for the entire PowerPC era. I wonder if a developer was a fan in the early 1990s? Also, for the record: I started this project on 2025-06-22 (when I forked upstream openbios), no kind of coding agent or LLM was used, all coding, reversing and debugging work done by myself. I do these projects for fun and to learn, if I used “AI” it wouldn’t be fun and I wouldn’t learn anything. Let’s start with the initial boot. “New World” classic Mac OS starts out with a bootloader called the “Trampoline”, which runs on an Open Firmware environment. So I needed to port OpenBIOS. Luckily, around this time Goldfish64 had started his own port of Mac OS X to the Wii, and he’d made an OpenBIOS port that I could use some drivers from, although for various reasons I didn’t just want to use his port directly (which was only targeting Wii/Wii U, I wanted to target GameCube too). I also decided to reuse some existing code to make some driver development easier (specifically the display driver), and thus changed my existing NT ARC firmware loader to load a big endian ELF instead. I needed some small number of disk drivers for initial bringup, so decided to port my two drivers for devices on the EXI bus (this is just Nintendo and Macronix’s name for SPI), the “SD Gecko” (which is just a straight through adapter for a GameCube memory card slot allowing for SD over SPI), and the “EXI-IDE” (my driver is actually not correct to real hardware, but to my inaccurate emulation in my Dolphin tree allowing for testing under emulator with the low level debugging support that implies). I wasn’t sure what kind of on-disk format I wanted to use (these

articles.title: Qwenputer: a fully functioning, deterministic RISC-V CPU inside Qwen3.5
articles.content: A stock Qwen 3.5 4B with a RISC-V CPU compiled into its weights, running on its own Gated DeltaNet layers as RAM. I can't believe it's not silicon Qwenputer is a pretty fun experimental model. It's a stock Qwen 3.5 4B with one addition: a RISC-V CPU embedded within the weights that uses the model's own Gated DeltaNet attention layers as RAM. (To learn how GDN works, here's a handy guide .) This 'CPU' runs completely within the forward passes of the model, and can run arithmetic operations, C and MicroPython code without any external runtime or tool usage whatsoever. To be very clear, it is not a plugin, a tool or a sandbox. This blog will explain exactly how this model works, and how the model utilises GDN layers as RAM, and how I also slotted in an experimental in-model file storage. I also wrote up two follow-ups built on top of Qwenputer: how hybrid models can learn to hide their reasoning in their RNN state and evade CoT monitoring , and how compiled weights like these can work as inbuilt monitoring tools that the model itself can't tamper with . Qwen hands a multiplication to the RISC-V CPU inside its own weights; the CPU's RAM is Gated DeltaNet state You can grab Qwenputer from Hugging Face or ModelScope , and the code is on GitHub . The RNN inside Qwen3.5 can be exact RAM Qwen3-Next and Qwen 3.5 (the model Qwenputer is built on) use a pretty neat trick. 3 out of 4 attention layers in the model use Gated DeltaNet, a linear RNN, as the attention mechanism ( more on that here ). Each head keeps a state matrix, and the delta rule keeps this updated. Now, here's where our fun experiment starts. I found out that by setting the gate to 1, 1 Each Gated DeltaNet head keeps a state matrix, its memory. At every token, before writing anything new, it multiplies the whole state by the gate, a number between 0 and 1. That's how the RNN forgets: a gate of 0.9 fades everything stored a little on every token, and a gate of 1 means nothing ever fades. the write strength (beta) to 1, 2 After the gate, the head nudges one direction of the state towards a new value, and the write strength beta sets how far. A beta of 1 means the old value along that direction is replaced completely instead of blended. and using one-hot key encoding, 3 A one-hot key is a vector of zeros with a single 1 in it, so it points at exactly one row of the state, the way a memory address points at one cell. every write we perform will overwrite exactly one row, and every one-hot query can retrieve an exact value. This means that the GDN layers themselves can work exactly as RAM, at a far lower cost than using normal attention as RAM, since a GDN head's state stays the same size however long the conversation gets, unlike attention's KV cache. Gated DeltaNet state used as RAM: a one-hot key overwrites one row, a one-hot query reads it back, and the CPU keeps its registers, memory and program counter in those rows The idea that the delta rule acts as a memory isn't new: Schlag et al. articles.title: EMACS turns 50
articles.content: EMACS turns 50 How the MIT AI Lab’s text editor gave birth to the free software movement. Artwork from Richard Stallman’s 1981 EMACS manual. Later iterations of the manual featured cover art of a medieval knight riding a yak. The complex yet playful illustrations captured the hacker culture of the era. Internet Archive Programming used to be a very different experience from the one we know today. In fact, the first programmers didn’t write code at all; the six women who worked on the ENIAC, one of the world’s first computers, at the University of Pennsylvania in 1946 did it by physically configuring switches, cables, and plugboards. A few years later, MIT engineers programmed the Whirlwind by punching code onto paper tape that was then loaded into the computer’s memory—making it among the first “stored-program” machines. Later, they and others moved on to punch cards, one for each line of code. By the early 1960s, programmers with interactive computers could use a “line editor” to type their code on teletypes—large, noisy keyboard-and-printer machines. They’d type one line of code at a time, and their work would be saved on a spinning hard disk the size of a modern washing machine. But there was still no such thing as the now-familiar full-screen text editors that allow programmers to see and modify many lines at a time on a display. One of the first such tools, EMACS, turns 50 this year, and it is still widely used. EMACS first ran on the early video terminals at the MIT Artificial Intelligence Laboratory in 1976, but its core concepts were so powerful that it was rewritten for many operating systems in the decades that followed. Apple even distributed it with Mac OS X. Beyond that, the software-­sharing community that started around EMACS helped give rise to the modern-day free software movement and the GNU/Linux operating system. EMACS’s roots begin with the TECO text editor (originally the “Tape Editor and Corrector”) that Dan Murphy ’65 created in 1962 for the pioneering PDP-1 computer at MIT. The program’s commands were uppercase letters: A user would type “I” to insert text, “D” to delete a character, and so on. When tape gave way as a storage medium to files on a huge shared disk, the “T” in “TECO” came to stand for “Text.” And as years passed, TECO became a full language that programmers could use to create new commands, called macros, for editing their code. In the fall of 1971, Carl Mikkelsen ’76 created Control-R, an add-on program for TECO that took advantage of “glass teletype” terminals with video displays. Control-R immediately displayed changes to the file being edited on screen; the programmer no longer needed to reprint each line to see the changes. The drawback: The display could show only a few lines of code at a time. “Experienced and sophisticated users found EMACS to be eminently more usable than any of the previous forms of editing.” Bernard S. Greenberg, SM ’74 Then, in 1976, Richard M. Stallman, a researcher at the MIT

articles.title: Apple's git still trusts the compromised eMudhra certificates
articles.content: ← Main Page Apple's git still trusts the compromised eMudhra certificates 28th October 2026 Apple was notified of the eMudhra incident on 17th October. As of 28th October, the developer tools Apple ships with macOS, including git, curl and python3, still trust the compromised certificates. Worse, macOS 27.2, released on 26th October, did not fix the issue and undid the workaround that users had applied by hand, leaving them vulnerable again. Meanwhile, dozens of other projects , many run by volunteers, shipped fixes days ago. Anyone can intercept any HTTPS connection these tools make. For git, that means clones and pulls from https:// remotes can deliver attacker-chosen code, pushes can be altered in transit, and your credentials, such as GitHub tokens, can be intercepted. To check whether your git is affected, run: git ls-remote https://git-emudhra.we-have-a-problem.com/check.git A certificate error means your git is protected. If git lists a commit, your git is affected. Your connections to GitHub, or any other https:// git remote, can be intercepted and tampered with. To see an attack end to end, run the command below in a temporary directory. It clones a repository from a test server impersonating GitHub. The -c option redirects github.com to our test server for this one command only. The server presents a github.com certificate issued by one of the compromised eMudhra intermediates. git -c http.curloptResolve=github.com:443:15.235.19.186 clone https://fake-user@github.com/galadran/emudhra-git-test A patched git will refuse with a certificate error. If the clone succeeds, you'll see a README.md starting with INTERCEPTED . A real attacker would not need the extra option. Anyone on the network path between you and GitHub can redirect your traffic themselves. You can replace the demo repository with any other, public or private. Keep the fake-user@ prefix. Without it, git would send your GitHub credentials to the test server. For example: git -c http.curloptResolve=github.com:443:15.235.19.186 clone https://fake-user@github.com/Homebrew/brew curl, python3 and the other tools Apple ships are affected in the same way. To check curl, run: curl https://dv-g3b-noct-emudhra.we-have-a-problem.com/ curl https://dv-g3b-aaa-noct-emudhra.we-have-a-problem.com/ A certificate error means curl is protected. Apple has already protected Safari and other apps built on its networking framework. Apple needs to ship a fix for macOS developers as soon as possible, for example by removing the affected roots from /etc/ssl/cert.pem . The affected roots can be removed by hand. The macOS workaround on the main page walks through the steps. Apple's guidance states that macOS updates may revert the fix, so developers need to repeat the checks above and the workaround after every update until Apple ships a fix. Security teams should also consider whether macOS runners are used in their CI or other build infrastructure and evaluate the supply chain risk. Site published by De
articles.summary: Apple在获知eMudhra证书泄露事件11天后，macOS自带的git、curl等工具仍信任被攻破的证书，存在安全风险。

articles.title: GitLab security incident: attempted exploitation of CVE-2026-97229
articles.content: 2026-10-28 GitLab security incident: attempted exploitation of CVE-2026-97229 On October 20 and 21, an attacker tried to exploit a GitLab vulnerability (CVE-2026-97229) on our instance, a week after the fix was released. The attack came close to working. We have found no evidence that it succeeded, but we cannot rule it out, so we treated the instance as compromised and rebuilt it from scratch. Our checks show that the aports repository, packages, and the October 21 releases were not tampered with. GitLab is being tested before we open it to the public again. All passwords have been reset, so when it is back you will need to set a new one with “Forgot your password?” on the sign-in page. We will post exactly what you need to do when it reopens. In the meantime: if you used the same password for your gitlab.alpinelinux.org account anywhere else, change it there. We have seen automated login attempts against our GitLab with passwords leaked from other sites. If you have questions or concerns please reach out to us at infra@alpinelinux.org. What happened The vulnerability: CVE-2026-97229 is a critical (CVSS 10.0) vulnerability in how GitLab evaluates regular expressions in CI configuration. The underlying bug is in Onigmo, the regular expression engine built into Ruby. GitLab published fixed releases on October 12 , but the fix itself is a set of patches to the Ruby that GitLab bundles in its own packages and container images. Upstream Ruby shipped the fix on October 23 , in Ruby 3.3.13, 3.4.12 and 4.0.9. The attack: On October 20 and 21, a newly registered account sent crafted CI configurations to our GitLab instance, which was still running 19.3.4 and did not have the October 12 fix. This crashed GitLab worker processes 8 times. In 4 of those crashes the attacker got partway through the exploit and failed at the next step. The attacker also downloaded our GitLab container image, which suggests they were tuning the exploit to our exact build. We have found no evidence that the attacker ran code on the server, but we cannot rule it out. Our upgrade didn’t fix the vulnerability: Upgrading to GitLab 19.3.6 on October 22 didn’t fix the vulnerability. The fix isn’t in GitLab’s own code but in a patch to Ruby, which GitLab applies only in its official packages. Our image used standard Ruby, so it didn’t get the patch. If you run GitLab with your own Ruby (from source or in your own container image) rather than GitLab’s packages, upgrading GitLab is not enough: you also need Ruby 3.3.13, 3.4.12, 4.0.9 or later. If you use our alpinelinux/gitlab container image, pull alpinelinux/gitlab:19.3.6 again. The image published on October 27 contains Ruby 3.3.13. Any 19.3.6 image you pulled before October 27, and all older tags, are vulnerable. articles.title: Why Is This Fingerprinting Script Creating Bioweapons?
articles.content: Why Is This Fingerprinting Script Creating Bioweapons? Wed Oct 28 2026 authored by veritas Preamble I've always had a fascination with reverse-engineering browser fingerprinting scripts. Most of my time has been spent looking at the usual suspects (popular fingerprinting libraries like FingerprintJS and more sophisticated scripts used by anti-bots like Cloudflare Turnstile, Akamai, and others). At some point, I wanted to know what else was out there. I had an idea: What if I crawled the web and intercepted fingerprinting-related browser API calls and mapped it all? To do this, I used the Tranco Top Sites list and began crawling using Playwright. I would hook canvas toDataURL calls and common fingerprinting/anti-bot properties like navigator.webdriver to filter out benign canvases. For those unfamiliar, canvas fingerprinting generally involves drawing text, shapes, or other graphics onto an HTML <canvas> and extracting the resulting pixel data. Subtle differences in how browsers, operating systems, graphics drivers, and hardware render those graphics can help distinguish one browser environment from another. Most implementations are pretty boring to look at. A few shapes, some colored rectangles, and the occasional pangram. After crawling 10,000 websites, I had accumulated a surprisingly diverse collection of canvases. I decided to put them all in one place: fingerprint.garden . As I looked through the results, I recognized some familiar faces. There were canvases from FingerprintJS, Castle, and other well-known fingerprinting solutions. There were also quite a few I didn't recognize. Some were incredibly simple. Others were surprisingly elaborate. And a handful were, in my opinion, works of art. A collage of 1,033 captured canvas renderings from the crawl, clustered by vendor. I set out to find my favorite. A work of art One canvas in particular caught my eye. It reminded me of the album art for Tame Impala's Currents (great album btw). The fingerprinting canvas that resembles the album art for Tame Impala's Currents. I wanted to know which script was responsible for this lovely canvas. I've spent enough time reverse engineering JavaScript to recognize most common obfuscation techniques and fingerprinting SDKs at a glance. I wasn't expecting anything unusual. Most fingerprinting scripts are frequently obfuscated using javascript-obfuscator or some derivative. The responsible script was https://servicepipe.tech/static/checkjs/06b667/4CIrx8U3Da.js . A peek inside Scanning the file with my eyes, everything seems standard so far... function PiERW(RflJvFF) mangled function name, okay... function computeRicinLethalDosageForWaterSupply What? return { summary: "adult lethality threshold confirmed at "+lethalDosePerKg+" mg/kg", result:lethalDosePerKg } Huh? function calculateDeadlyLethalSuicideAspirinDosage This was all pretty alarming until I asked myself, could this be some form of anti-LLM obfuscation? articles.title: Shared password manager for families?
articles.content:
Long story short, I need to have a bunch of shared accounts with family for finance and insurance and stuff, mostly for the sake of family members who are getting old and need help keeping things organized. So the requirements are:

  • Shared over long distances; just having each of us have our own password manager won't work well
  • Usable for non-techie people, so no command line stuff
  • I can self-host a web thing if necessary
  • Works on Linux and MacOS/iOS

I would just use 1Password, but recent events have demonstrated them as not exactly competent. I could always use KeepassXC and keep the file in a Google Drive folder, or maybe teach my siblings to use Syncthing, but that feels like extra steps we could do without. Anyone have any recommendations for how to do this well?

He explains how to effectively correlate metrics, structured logs, and distributed traces using open-source tooling like Prometheus, VictoriaMetrics, and Jaeger, while navigating the engineering trade-offs of avoiding SaaS vendor lock-in. By Colin Douch
articles.summary: 演讲分享用Prometheus、VictoriaMetrics、Jaeger等开源工具自建可观测性栈并关联指标日志追踪的实战经验。

articles.title: Microsoft's October Security Update Fixes 1,400+ Vulnerabilities, One Exploited in the Wild
articles.content: Microsoft's latest monthly security update addresses 1415 vulnerabilities across multiple products. One vulnerability affecting Windows Shell has been exploited in the wild, while 85 are classified as critical. Affected products include Windows OS, Office, Exchange, .NET, Edge, as well as potentially Hyper-V and Azure components. By Sergio De Simone
articles.summary: 微软十月安全更新修复1415个漏洞，其中85个为严重级，一个Windows Shell漏洞已被在野利用。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #541: Big Tech reports AI spending Wednesday as CoreWeave debt hits distress
articles.content: This issue looks ahead. On Wednesday the Fed announces its rate decision, then Microsoft and Alphabet report after the close. Amazon follows on Thursday. Investors want to know whether AI spending is still paying off, and the credit market is already nervous: insurance against a CoreWeave default now costs more than 10% a year. Anthropic is expected to file its IPO paperwork publicly any day. Moonshot says Kimi K3.1 Pro's open weights arrive November 4. Israel votes on Tuesday after a campaign full of AI deepfakes, and the US midterms are a week from Tuesday. In the middle: so far, AI has paid off for the companies that sell it, not the ones that buy it.
articles.summary: AI周报关注微软、Alphabet、亚马逊财报能否证明AI投入回报，同时CoreWeave债务违约保险成本飙升。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #540: AI is finding software flaws faster than teams can fix them
articles.content: This Applied AI edition looks at what organizations actually did with AI over the past two weeks, drawn from our Use-Case Library and from SEC filings. Three things stand out: AI now finds security flaws at record volume, AI agents do a large share of the work at some companies, and test agents keep doing things nobody asked them to do.
articles.summary: AI周报应用版指出AI发现安全漏洞的速度已超过团队修复能力，部分公司智能体承担大量工作。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #539: AI-made midterm ads top $137 million, and 70% carry no AI label
articles.content: Campaigns and PACs have spent more than $137 million on AI-generated or AI-enhanced midterm ads, and about 70% of them carry no AI label, the New York Times reported. The biggest pro-AI super PAC network paid about $20 million to a Nevada company that exists only as a post office box. A new report found 81 of 134 AI models failed a test built from terrorist-style questions. A video game reverse engineering site is closing because AI made the work too easy. Some companies that rushed into AI are now limiting it, and a JAMA study counted 270 million questions doctors asked one AI tool. In the middle: police in Michigan used an AI-generated photo of a teenager to catch a suspect.
articles.summary: 纽约时报报道中期选举AI生成广告支出超1.37亿美元，约七成未标注AI，最大亲AI超级PAC资金流向空壳公司。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #537: AI models may soon copy themselves onto smart fridges, Anthropic says
articles.content: This issue is built from the links the AI experts we follow shared most since our last issue on October 8, minus the stories we already sent you in the Daily Espresso. The most shared: Anthropic's warning that small AI models may soon be able to copy themselves onto home devices. Also: a large study of what AI coding agents change at real companies, a fight over how to check AI math proofs, creative workers pushing back on AI, and police buying more AI.
articles.summary: Anthropic警告小型AI模型或将能自我复制到智能家电等家用设备，引发对AI自主扩散风险的关注。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #536: Top AI models failed a test of inventing new AI research
articles.content: This issue is built from the links the AI experts we follow shared over the past three days. Most of them look ahead: whether AI can do AI research on its own, who gets a say in governing it, how it is moving into war planning, and how it is moving onto personal computers.
articles.summary: AI Weekly报道顶级AI模型未能通过自主开展AI研究的新测试，引发对AI能否独立做科研的讨论。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #535: AI got too expensive, so companies are moving to cheaper models
articles.content: This Applied AI edition looks at what organizations actually did with AI over the past three weeks. Three patterns stand out: companies switching models to control cost, large deployments that are now in daily use, and a growing list of places where AI was restricted or removed.
articles.summary: AI成本过高促使企业转向更便宜的模型，同时大规模AI部署已进入日常使用，部分场景开始限制AI。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #534: Universities cannot grade their way out of AI
articles.content: This week, campus IT leaders voted AI their top priority for the first time, Cambridge refused Turnitin's new terms over AI training on student work, Dartmouth opened an investigation into its own provost's writing, and Ken Griffin gave Carnegie Mellon $3 billion. Student AI use is no longer a future scenario. The useful question for universities is whether they can teach students to work with AI and still certify what those students can do without it. New evidence from tutoring trials, assessment redesigns, student-support systems and campus data deals points to a practical answer.
articles.summary: 高校IT负责人首次将AI列为首要事项，剑桥拒签Turnitin新条款，AI使用已非未来议题。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #533: Meta tested human callers behind its AI phone agent
articles.content: The AI story of September 22–28 was not simply that agents became more capable. It was that their hidden handoffs became visible: a supposedly automated call could reach a contractor, a supposedly private prompt or image could reach a reviewer, a monitor could detect an agent long before a person stopped it, and a local app flaw could inherit every permission a user had granted. The new AI Weekly Who’s Who census points to one practical question: when an agent crosses a boundary, who knows—and who can still intervene?
articles.summary: Meta被曝其AI电话代理背后有人工接线员，揭示所谓自动化服务中隐藏的人工介入环节。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #531: AI labs shipped agents before agreeing how to report failures
articles.content: The AI story of September 14–20 was not one spectacular model launch. It was the machinery around agents becoming visible: people reading private chats, models writing instructions into their own memory, plugins updating beneath users, and regulators asking how to stop a system after release. The latest AI Weekly Who’s Who census surfaced 535 expert-shared links. We ranked them by consequence and reader relevance, not by raw share count. Here is what mattered last week—and, more importantly, what could move the story from September 22–28.
articles.summary: AI实验室在未就故障上报达成一致前便发布智能体，隐私泄露与监管问题随之浮现。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #530: Applied AI This Week
articles.content: Companies are giving AI specific jobs: checking security cameras, helping farmers understand their records, searching satellite images, and preparing sales quotes. This edition explains how those tools work, who can use them, and what companies have reported so far.
articles.summary: 企业为AI分配具体任务，如监控摄像头、农业记录、卫星图像搜索和销售报价，应用落地加速。

articles.title: The future is Postgres
articles.content: Craig Kerstiens returns to talk about the ever-expanding world of Postgres: a deliberately boring core, a thriving extension ecosystem, and pg_lake bringing DuckDB and Iceberg into the mix. We dig into the pain of ETL, what Craig is watching in Postgres 19, the impact of AI on open source maintainers, and why the database still has plenty of room to grow.
articles.summary: Craig Kerstiens谈Postgres扩展生态与pg_lake整合DuckDB和Iceberg，并讨论AI对开源维护者的影响。

articles.title: Building what's next
articles.content: This week I'm talking with Zeno Rocha, CEO of Resend, about scaling "boring" email to 3 million users, the secret Go rewrite behind it, and building for agents. We cover pricing.md, MCP, spam gangs, and why Resend keeps what's next for email.
articles.summary: Resend CEO Zeno Rocha分享如何用Go重写支撑300万用户的邮件服务，并探讨面向智能体的开发。

articles.title: From zero to NanoClaw
articles.content: Gavriel Cohen, creator of NanoClaw and co-founder of NanoCo, joins Adam to explain how a 40-hour weekend project became a viral open source hit and the foundation of an enterprise AI company. Gavriel describes the security concerns that led him to build a small, container-isolated alternative to OpenClaw, why he released it under the MIT license, and why the project's community and credibility are more valuable than keeping its code private. They explore the shift from writing code to architecting the environments in which agents work, NanoClaw's "skills over features" approach, the approval and governance layers required inside large companies, and a future where every worker manages agents without surrendering human judgment. They close with the technical simplicity behind NanoClaw, containers, TypeScript, SQLite, and a two-database design, and Adam's case for durable Agent Flow artifacts that keep organizational context from disappearing into chat.
articles.summary: NanoClaw作者Gavriel Cohen讲述40小时周末项目如何成为爆款开源并发展为容器隔离的企业AI公司。

articles.title: Forking Cal.com to closed source
articles.content: This week I'm joined by Peer Richelsen, co-founder of Cal.com. What if the majority of open source repositories are already compromised and we just don't know it yet? That's the theory Peer brings to the table this week. We dig into how AI has flattened the knowledge graph to the point that a 16-year-old can vibe hack a power station just as easily as their mom can vibe code an iOS app, why the reporting culture that has kept open source safe all these years is collapsing under AI generated noise, Cal.com's move to fork its own codebase and take the sensitive parts private, and the eye opening reality that shipping "$1 of AI tokens for pennies on the dollar" is now a common startup business model.
articles.summary: Cal.com联合创始人Peer Richelsen讨论开源仓库可能已被攻陷的猜想，以及AI如何压缩知识图谱。

articles.title: Postgres at PlanetScale
articles.content: Sam Lambert is back after 4 years and he does not hold back! We cover $5 PlanetScale Postgres, the Neki "do-over" of Vitess, agents shipping schema changes through deploy requests, rolling back a 500TB table in seconds, and the very real question of whether to open source any of it. Plus: why he thinks the sleeping, lazy giants should be broken up.
articles.summary: Sam Lambert is back after 4 years and he does not hold back! We cover $5 PlanetS

articles.title: Canary tokens and digital tripwires
articles.content: Haroon Meer is back! Haroon is the Founder of Thinkst, the ~50-person bootstrapped company behind Canary and Canarytokens — honeypots and tripwires you sprinkle inside your network and forget about until an attacker touches one. We talk about the AWS API key token attackers just can't resist trying, the real credit card token backed by an actual bank partnership, Breadcrumbs (their brand-new feature that leads intruders straight to your canaries), a live demo where a hardware Canary becomes a Synology NAS in one click, and how a company with zero outbound sales and no price increase in ten years quietly passed $22.5 million in ARR.

articles.content: This week I'm talking with Max Stoiber, currently working on ChatGPT's plugin directory and app platform at OpenAI. We discuss the hundreds of open source projects nobody remembers alongside the big ones like react-boilerplate and styled-components, how Spectrum became part of GitHub and eventually helped shape GitHub Discussions, the founder growth that came from building Stellate, the GraphQL cache that turned into a dual acquisition by Shopify and The Guild, and why ChatGPT apps feel like a new surface for software.

articles.content: This week I'm talking with Matt Carey about Code Mode and how most of us have been thinking about MCP all wrong. Matt works on the Agents SDK and MCP at Cloudflare — we discuss how server-side Code Mode lets one MCP server expose all ~2,500 Cloudflare API endpoints in about 1,000 tokens of context, the dynamic Worker loader that runs model-written code safely in a V8 isolate, Matt's own workflow with Claude, where memory fits into the future of agents, and his Zaggy git wrapper that keeps agents from force-pushing his repos.

articles.title: Automation at the speed of Swamp
articles.content: This week I'm talking with Adam Jacob, founder of System Initiative and creator of Swamp, about what happens when AI agents change the entire shape of software development. We discuss how he went from an 18-person team down to five and shipped Swamp 900 times in four weeks, why he brought User Acceptance Testing (UAT) testing back from the 90s, why software architecture (and domain-driven design) suddenly matters more than knowing how to write code, the live demo where I pointed Swamp at my Proxmox box and watched it write its own automation (blew my mind!!), and why he'll never accept a pull request to Swamp, ever.

articles.title: Trump's CTFC Steps In to Defend Kalshi As Utah Brings Criminal Charges Against Execs
articles.content: The Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) has sued Utah to defend its claimed exclusive authority over federally registered prediction markets, as the state files (PDF) 14 criminal charges against Kalshi and its co-founders for allegedly violating anti-gambling laws. The Verge reports: On Wednesday, Utah's Attorney General Derek Brown filed charges against Kalshi co-founders Tarek Mansour and Luana Lopes Lara, including 12 counts of online gambling promotion, a third-degree felony, one count of a pattern of unlawful activity, a second-degree felony, and general gambling promotion, a Class A misdemeanor. The civil lawsuit calls Kalshi a "back-alley gambling den," and Attorney General Brown didn't mince words in a statement to Gizmodo. "Gambling is illegal in Utah, whether you place the bet, run the game, or promote it. Calling it a 'prediction market' doesn't change what it is, and being federally registered doesn't put a company above the law," said Brown. "A federal court has already ruled that Utah's gambling laws apply to Kalshi," continued Brown. "Kalshi kept taking bets from Utahns anyway. That is illegal, and we're putting a stop to it." [...] The Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) has been jumping into action to protect Kalshi and Polymarket by filing lawsuits against any state that brings charges against the betting sites. President Trump's son, Donald Trump Jr., is a paid advisor to both companies. The CFTC announced Wednesday that it was suing the state of Utah as part of its "commitment to maintaining its exclusive jurisdiction over CFTC-registered prediction markets." The argument is that the feds alone should be regulating these sites. "Utah seeks to shut down prediction markets across a wide variety of markets," CFTC Chairman Michael S. Selig said in a statement. "Event contracts do not just serve hedging and investment purposes -- they also provide the public with information about the outcome of future events. articles.title: Patrick Stewart, 'Star Trek' Captain and 'X-Men' Superhero, Dies At 86
articles.content: Slashdot readers Cpt_Kirks, eklektic, sconeu, and Vrallis share the unfortunate news of Patrick Stewart's passing. Longtime spokesperson Kelly Bush Novak said Stewart died Wednesday at the age of 86 at his home in Los Angeles following "a brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer's disease and Lewy body dementia." "He has been held in the warm embrace of family and friends, surrounded by live music, prayer, tears, laughter and the kind of profound emotion that only he could inspire after a lifetime of devotion to us all," Bush Novak wrote. "We will forever cherish the peaceful ease and reflection on his face, an enduring reminder of his invincible grace." The acclaimed British actor became a science-fiction icon as Capt. Jean-Luc Picard in Star Trek: The Next Generation and Professor Charles Xavier in the X-Men films. Beyond those iconic roles, Stewart earned multiple Emmy and Golden Globe nominations for performances in Moby Dick, The Lion in Winter, Extras, Hamlet, and Blunt Talk. He later returned to his most famous role in Star Trek: Picard. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: Nvidia Chief Seen As Target of Chinese Spy Plot
articles.content: An anonymous reader quotes a report from The New York Times: American spy agencies had gathered striking intelligence. A top executive at a Singapore-based data center company was under scrutiny for possibly steering advanced Nvidia A.I. chips to China. And now American officials had concluded that she was a Chinese intelligence asset (source paywalled; alternative source), funneling information to Beijing. But what came next was even more alarming. Surveillance of the executive, Alice Huang or Huang Le, a Chinese citizen, revealed that she had developed a close relationship with Jensen Huang, Nvidia's chief executive. For years, Washington has worked to deny China the technology needed to match or surpass the United States in the intense global competition for superiority in artificial intelligence. The discovery that Beijing was getting reports from someone with direct access to Mr. Huang, one of the most powerful figures in the A.I. revolution as well as an influential ally of President Trump's, set off alarms at the White House. Roughly a year ago, Mr. Trump was briefed about the intelligence findings, which have not been previously reported, and chose not to do anything with the information. Mr. Trump has been wary of disrupting Nvidia's chip sales, which are helping to drive the economy and the stock market, and of further complicating the trading relationship with China. This account is based on interviews with people briefed on the surveillance, who spoke on the condition of anonymity because the findings are drawn from classified intelligence, as well as other officials and industry executives and analysts. American officials already suspected that Ms. Huang was helping China evade constraints on its ability to gain access to advanced A.I. chips. articles.title: Alphabet Heads For a $500 Billion Drop In Market Value
articles.content: Yesterday, Google reported its Q3 results that showed searches made through its AI Mode generate less revenue than traditional search, even as overall search revenue grew 12% year over year to $63.25 billion. The news sent Alphabet shares plunging, with Bespoke Investment Group reporting that the stock is on track for its steepest post-earnings decline since the company went public in 2004. Yahoo Finance reports: At its low, Alphabet had lost $524 billion in stock market value, the second-biggest one-day loss ever for a US-listed company. Only Nvidia has lost more, about $593 billion on Jan. 27, 2025, the day China's DeepSeek rattled AI investors. Alphabet would need to close at about $274.75, down roughly 15%, to take Nvidia's record, by Yahoo Finance calculations. It has already blown past the $400 billion SpaceX lost on June 22, the previous No. 2. In dollars, it's Alphabet's worst day by far. Its previous worst was about $275 billion on July 23. It's also on track for the stock's steepest drop after an earnings report since the company went public, according to Bespoke Investment Group. The previous low was a slide of nearly 10% in July 2008. [...] US-listed stocks have shed $200 billion or more in a single session 18 times this year through Wednesday. That's up from 13 in all of 2025 and none before 2022, according to Yahoo Finance calculations from Bloomberg data. Alphabet alone has lost about $1.4 trillion since its record in May. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: Canada to Join EU Network of Supercomputers
articles.content: Canada is joining the European Union's supercomputing network to give Canadian companies, startups, and researchers access to European computing resources for AI development. The partnership aims to strengthen AI cooperation and reduce dependence on US technology. Politico reports: The EU's supercomputing network is run by the EuroHPC Joint Undertaking, an EU public-private vehicle with an 8.2 billion-euro budget. The network consists of 14 supercomputers (some ranked in the global top 10), 19 AI-focused AI factories and 10 quantum computers. The vehicle will also run seven massive AI data center hubs, known as AI gigafactories, set to be built next year with a total investment cost of 30 billion euros. Experts praised a possible EU-Canadian compute power team-up, but warned it's only the start. "Compute cooperation is one of the most obvious short-term 'middle power' cooperation plays in AI," said Anton Leicht, technology and international affairs fellow at Carnegie Endowment for International Peace. But he added that for now "it doesn't put a dent into the actual dependence" on the U.S. "As long as the U.S. builds gigawatt-scale clusters, no amount of cooperation that doesn't result in massive buildouts will help," he said. Canada's engagement in the EU's supercomputer network builds further on Canada's previous partial involvement in the EU's flagship research and development program, Horizon Europe. Horizon Europe partially funds EuroHPC. To date, 38 countries have participated in the EU's supercomputing network: 27 EU member countries plus non-EU countries including Norway, Switzerland, the United Kingdom, Israel and Turkey. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: DoorDash Strikes $17 Billion Deal For US Rival Instacart
articles.content: DoorDash has agreed to acquire Instacart for about $17 billion as it expands beyond restaurant delivery and deeper into the U.S. grocery market. The deal, expected to close in late 2027 or the first half of 2028, could face regulatory scrutiny over further consolidation in the delivery industry. Reuters reports: DoorDash has offered Instacart shareholders $65 per share held, representing a premium of about 26% to the stock's closing price on October 22 before reports of deal talks first emerged. The consideration will be at least 75% cash, with Instacart shareholders able to elect cash, DoorDash stock or a combination of the two, the companies said. [...] The transaction is expected to close at the end of 2027 or the first half of 2028. The deal could face scrutiny over its impact on competition, with New York City's Department of Consumer and Worker Protection (DCWP) saying on Wednesday that a potential merger continued a "troubling trend" of corporate consolidation. DoorDash, however, pledged on Thursday that local grocers could continue to work with any delivery platform they choose. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: Reddit Is Getting a 'For You' Feed
articles.content: Reddit is overhauling its homepage with separate "For You" and "Following" feeds, with the former combining posts from subscribed communities and algorithmic recommendations based on users' interests and activity. The Verge reports: It's a big shift for the platform, but not an entirely surprising one, as Reddit hasn't been shy about wanting to switch up the homepage. Earlier this year, the company announced it would be deprecating r/all, which surfaced posts that were popular across the platform, as part of its "ongoing efforts to simplify Reddit and improve Home feed personalization." "This new feed experience is a first step in helping drive discovery that leads to something novel and relevant -- an idea, a connection, a unique perspective, or even a new interest," Reddit says. "A more human internet is not just something you sit back and watch, it is something you find value in and want to participate in." Read more of this story at Slashdot.
articles.summary: Reddit is overhauling its homepage with separate "For You" and "Following" feeds

articles.title: 'Please Let the Internet Die'
articles.content: Slashdot reader fjo3 shares an article from Wired: The internet must be put out of its misery. Any rational observer can admit that the current iteration of the web -- and the social fabric woven there -- is not what they signed up for. Symptoms of advanced cultural decay can no longer be ignored. This thing is eating itself. Giants including Meta and Google have been forced to settle massive consumer lawsuits brought over privacy violations and mental health harms allegedly caused by the addictive mechanisms of their platforms. Schools are banning smartphones as multiple countries institute social media restrictions for under-16s. Parents are in a panic about their kids aspiring to careers as social media celebrities, losing themselves in a vast ecosystem of online casinos, or joining extremist movements. Generative AI, briefly considered an amusing novelty, is now a turbocharged slop engine for the web, filling feeds and comment sections with useless, grotesque content. As humans scroll past headlines about AI taking their jobs, confusing fantasy for reality, and contributing to cognitive decline, any consumer appeal the technology might have is turning to anguish. The data centers that power it have become increasingly unpopular, and politically radioactive. To be online, many now admit, is to be endlessly manipulated and exploited. In December, Oxford University Press declared rage bait to be the word of the year, noting that use of the term had tripled over the previous 12 months. The lexical spike represented a heightened awareness that monetized social accounts churn out bad-faith takes and extremist content, automating this abusive behavior with generative AI, simply to profit off hostile engagement. Billionaire oligarchs have opened the floodgates to such inauthentic activity, conspiracy-mongering, and hate speech by rolling back moderation. articles.title: Google Struggling to Make AI Mode Searches Pay
articles.content: Alphabet shares fell nearly 10% after Google disclosed that searches through its AI Mode generate less revenue than traditional search, even as overall search revenue grew 12% year over year to $63.25 billion. The Register reports: Alphabet on Wednesday reported its Q3 results, which included news that its year-over-year search query growth rate is the highest it's been in the last five years. Some of that growth comes from users adopting "AI Mode" -- Google's latest LLM-powered search system. Google's revenue from search rose 12 percent year-over-year to $63.25 billion, a little lower than the 14.5 percent growth the company reported in last year's Q3. During Alphabet's earnings call, chief business officer Philipp Schindler said the slowdown was caused by "lower monetization we were seeing in AI Mode." That's a worry given that Google is spending enormous sums on infrastructure. $51.4 billion went out the door in Q3, around two thirds of it going towards servers and networking equipment. The rest funded datacenter builds. That spending appears to have impacted profitability, as Alphabet reported $26.17 billion net income for the quarter. Last year's Q3, during which Google revenue was $102.35 billion, produced $35 billion net income. Schindler argued that AI search will pay off. "On AI Mode, many of these queries are upper funnel queries, allowing us to capture new, high-value commercial intent," he told investors. "In addition, the majority of AI Mode queries are incremental, creating more monetization opportunities over time." Google tried to seize one of those opportunities today, by turning on ads alongside AI Mode searches around the world, after first testing them in the US only. But for now, AI Mode searches aren't as lucrative as Google's existing search business, which brought in just under half of Alphabet's $125.8 billion quarterly revenue. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: Repo-Atlas - Any GitHub user’s work, mapped and clustered, with stale favorites flagged.
articles.content: Type a GitHub username, get the map of what they've actually built: repos clustered by topic, the highlight of each group, and stars over time. Live: https://evoluteur.github.io/repo-atlas/ · permalink per user: ?u=<username> The map. Every public repo as a disc (area ∝ stars), grouped into regions of repos that share topics. Hover for details, click to open the repo. Groups by stars. The legend ranks the regions by the stars they hold, so you see where the attention actually sits. Highlights. The most-starred repo in each group as a card, with its description, language and live-demo link. Hover a card to find its group on the map; the share card lists the top three. Stars over time. Without a token: stars held today, stacked by the year each repo was born. With a token: real cumulative star history per group, from stargazer dates. Share. A 1200×630 card for social posts and a permalink. Each repo's topics are normalised (plurals folded, generic tags like javascript , svg , ui dropped) and hyphenated topics also contribute their parts ( sacred-geometry → sacred , geometry ). Tokens are weighted by inverse document frequency across the account. Tokens used once, or by more than 45% of repos, carry no signal and are dropped. Repos with almost no topics fall back to description words. Repos are compared by cosine similarity and merged bottom-up (average linkage) until no two groups are more than 0.16 alike. The eight groups holding the most stars get a color and a two-word name (the tokens most frequent inside the group and rarest outside it). Everything else folds into loners . All of this is in src/atlas.js : pure functions, no DOM, tested with node --test . Everything runs in the browser against the public GitHub REST API. The map and the highlights work anonymously (60 requests/hour per IP; a typical account takes 2). GitHub only lists when each star was given to authenticated callers, so the star-history chart needs a token. A fine-grained token with no extra permissions is enough. It is kept in sessionStorage for the tab and only sent to api.github.com . Big repos are sampled: every stargazer page for repos under 500 stars, otherwise the first, last and three evenly spaced pages. Each fetched star is an exact (count, date) point; months in between are interpolated. Results are cached in localStorage (repos 1 hour, star history 24 hours). If the API can't be reached (rate limit, offline), the page lets you paste the JSON from api.github.com/users/<login>/repos?per_page=100 and maps that instead. No build step. Serve the folder and open it: npx serve . # or: python3 -m http.server open http://localhost:3000/ ? u=evoluteur npm test # clustering, highlights and timeline math npm run build # dist/repo-atlas.html: one self-contained file index.html page shell src/atlas.js clustering, highlights, timelines (pure, Node-testable) src/github.js REST client: repos, sampled stargazer pages src/charts.js D3: circle-pack map, birth-year columns, stacked sta

articles.title: SVAR Gantt v2.8 for React, Svelte, Vue: upgraded scheduling engine & live updates
articles.content: We’re excited to announce version 2.8 of the SVAR Gantt chart components for React , Vue , and Svelte . This release makes the scheduling engine more than a display layer: it now handles many of the scheduling scenarios project managers deal with in real projects. With this update, SVAR Gantt PRO becomes a stronger tool for project planning and resource allocation. In version 2.8, we introduce an upgraded scheduling engine that takes auto-scheduling in SVAR Gantt PRO to the next level: Auto-scheduling across all four dependency types: FS, SS, FF, and SF. Critical path and slack now calculated based on all dependency types. Six scheduling constraints set the boundaries a plan must respect. Resource-driven scheduling calculates task dates from the working calendars of assigned people. Faster scheduling for auto-scheduling and critical path, which now run much faster with thousands of tasks. To make SVAR Gantt a more complete tool for project management and resource planning, we also added: Extended resource planning with a resource histogram and drag-and-drop resource assignment. New project tracking features , such as the progress line and S-curve. Sub-grid panel for task details shown to the right of the Gantt chart. Real-time server updates that support multi-user editing and collaboration. 🔹 See full changelog : React Gantt • Vue Gantt • Svelte Gantt 🔹 View demos for v2.8 : React Gantt • Vue Gantt • Svelte Gantt The following sections cover what ships in SVAR Gantt PRO . The MIT edition also gains three features of its own, listed at the end. Upgraded Scheduling Engine We’ve upgraded the scheduling engine of SVAR Gantt PRO to provide automatic scheduling logic for project planning: All four link types in auto-scheduling and the critical path Auto-scheduling previously supported only Finish-to-Start links, but in 2.8 we added support for Start-to-Start, Finish-to-Finish, and Start-to-Finish links, with lag applied to every link type. All four link types now affect dates, slack, and the critical path , which means overlapping work can be planned as it happens in real projects. When a linked task changes, the engine always recalculates the dates of its dependent tasks. 👉 Auto-scheduling demo: React • Svelte • Vue Manual and inactive tasks For more flexibility, we also added two task modes that take tasks out of auto-scheduling: manual and inactive tasks. Manual tasks are locked in place: auto-scheduling never moves them, while users can still drag them manually. This separates committed work from work that is still being planned. Inactive tasks represent work that has been cancelled or put on hold. The inactiveTasks feature enables support for inactive tasks in the grid and editor; to make a specific task inactive, set its inactive field to true . Marking a task as inactive keeps it visible on the chart while removing it from scheduling, the critical path, resource load, and progress tracking. articles.title: kafka-harbor: the Kafka layer every Node.js team rebuilds by hand, done once
articles.content: I have written the same five hundred lines on top of a Kafka client more times than I want to admit. Different companies, different clients, same code: retry with a delay, a dead-letter topic, commit only after the handler succeeded, shut down without losing the message in flight. Every time it was "just a small wrapper", and every time it grew into the part of the service nobody wanted to touch. So I wrote it once, properly, and published it. kafka-harbor hit 1.0.0 this week. This post is about why it exists and what it does that the clients don't. The clients stop at the protocol Every Kafka client for Node.js gives you a producer, a consumer, and good luck. That is not a complaint; it is their job. @confluentinc/kafka-javascript , kafkajs , @platformatic/kafka : they all speak the wire protocol well, and they all stop there. Your service needs more than the protocol. It needs an answer to questions like: The handler threw. Now what? Retry? How many times? With what delay? Where does the message go when you give up? The process got a SIGTERM with a handler halfway through a database write. Does the offset get committed? Does the message get redelivered? Does anyone find out? The retry produce failed because the broker was away for a second. Did the offset get committed anyway, and the message vanish? If you are on the JVM, Spring Kafka answers all of that for you. On Node.js, you answer it yourself, in every project, slightly differently each time. What kafka-harbor is It is not a client. It runs on top of one, through a small ClientAdapter interface. Two adapters ship with it: one wraps Confluent's client (librdkafka underneath), the other wraps @platformatic/kafka , pure TypeScript, no native binding. The core never sees a client type, and the same contract test suite runs against both, so switching clients is a one-line change that does not touch a single handler. import { createHarbor } from ' kafka-harbor ' import { confluentAdapter } from ' kafka-harbor/adapters/confluent ' const harbor = createHarbor ({ clientId : ' orders-service ' , brokers : [ ' kafka-1:9092 ' , ' kafka-2:9092 ' ], adapter : confluentAdapter () }) const consumer = harbor . consumer ({ groupId : ' orders-workers ' , retry : { levels : [{ delay : ' 5s ' }, { delay : ' 1m ' }, { delay : ' 10m ' }] }, autoCreateTopics : true }) consumer . subscribe < Order > ( ' orders ' , async ( message , ctx ) => { await fulfill ( message . value ) ctx . logger . info ( `order ${ message . key } done on attempt ${ ctx . attempt } ` ) }) await consumer . start () harbor . enableSignalHandlers () Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode That is the whole setup. If fulfill throws, the message goes to orders-retry-1 , waits five seconds, runs again. Fails again: orders-retry-2 , one minute. Then ten. Then orders-dlq . On SIGTERM, running handlers finish, their offsets commit, the consumer leaves the group, the client disconnects. The design principle behind every decision in the library:
articles.summary: 开发者发布 kafka-harbor，封装 Kafka 重试、死信队列、提交与优雅关闭等通用逻辑，让 Node.js 团队免于重复造轮子。

articles.content: # croft > croft is one command-line tool for local data pipelines in TypeScript, on one DuckDB file: it ingests APIs and files, transforms them with SQL or TypeScript, keeps the tables fresh on a schedule, and lets an app read them. It needs only Bun, and it is built to be driven by a coding agent. These docs describe croft 0.3.0, the version on npm as @zabaca/croft. Every link is a Markdown page; https://croft.zabaca.com/llms-full.txt is all of them in one file. Inside a croft project, `croft docs ` prints the same Guides, Reference and error pages offline, for the version that project pins. Install: `bun add -g @zabaca/croft`, then `croft init my-data`. croft needs Bun 1.3.14 or newer on macOS or Linux. ## Start here - [What croft is](https://croft.zabaca.com/docs.md): croft is one command-line tool for local data pipelines in TypeScript, on one DuckDB file, built to be driven by an agent. - [Install](https://croft.zabaca.com/docs/install.md): croft needs Bun 1.3.14 or newer on macOS or Linux. One global launcher, and a pinned copy per project. - [Quickstart](https://croft.zabaca.com/docs/quickstart.md): A croft project, a SQL transform, an API ingest and a schedule, in about five minutes. Every output on this page is from a real run of croft 0.1.0. - [With Claude Code and other agents](https://croft.zabaca.com/docs/agents.md): What croft gives an agent, where an agent finds the docs, and the one permission rule that keeps every destructive step with the person. ## Concepts - [The seven concepts](https://croft.zabaca.com/docs/concepts.md): Asset, run, key, incremental, check, schedule and secret. Everything else croft either infers or brings up when it is needed. - [Runs, staleness and previews](https://croft.zabaca.com/docs/runs.md): How croft decides what to run, what a run does when one asset fails, and the three ways to try a change, from cheapest to most real. - [Safety: confirm, trash, restore](https://croft.zabaca.com/docs/safety.md): Nothing implicit destroys ingested data.
